en: The Recorded Sayings of Layman Pang, Volume One.
Compiled by Yu Di, Military Commissioner; reprinted by Upāsaka Shideng.
The layman Pang Yun of Xiangzhou, courtesy name Daoxuan, was a native of Hengyang County in Hengzhou.
His family had long been established in the Confucian profession, but from his youth he awakened to the weariness of worldly toil and resolved to seek the ultimate truth.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he visited Master Shitou and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Shitou covered his mouth with his hand, and Pang Yun attained sudden enlightenment.
One day, Shitou asked, "Since you first met this old monk, how have you conducted yourself in your daily activities?
The scholar said, "If you ask about my daily activities, there is no opening for words. Shitou said, "I knew you were like this before I even asked you."
The Master then presented a verse, saying: "In daily activities there is no distinction; Only I myself am in harmony. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting;

In every place there is no discord or conflict. Who assigns the titles 'red' and 'purple'? Mountains and hills are free from even a speck of dust. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions— [All are spontaneously present.]”
He transported water and carried firewood. Daotai asked him, "Do you wish to wear black robes or white robes? The scholar replied, "I wish to follow what I admire.
Thereupon, he did not shave his head or dye his hair.
Later, the layman went to Jiangxi to visit Master Mazu. He asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River with a single draught, and then I will tell you.

At these words, the layman suddenly realized the profound essence of the teaching. He then presented a verse containing the line, "With a mind, one passes the imperial examination of emptiness," and remained there to stay.

Having served him for two years, he offered this verse: "A man has no son to marry; A woman has no daughter to wed. The whole family sits in a circle, Together discussing the discourse on non-arising.
One day, the scholar again asked the Patriarch: "The person who is originally present is not obscure;

I ask the Master to cast his eyes high. The Patriarch looked straight down. The scholar said: "This is a single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it with marvelous skill. The Patriarch looked straight ahead.
The Master looked up. The scholar prostrated himself. The Patriarch returned to his quarters, and the scholar followed behind him, saying, "Just now, my cleverness turned into clumsiness.
One day, the scholar asked the Patriarch again, "As for the saying, 'Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-hu vessel'—what is the principle behind this?"
The Patriarch said: "Here there is neither water nor boat; what need is there to speak of sinews and bones?
The Layman went to Zen Master Yaoshan, who asked: "Within the One Vehicle, can this matter be contained?"
The layman said, "I merely strive day by day for a few pints or quarts; I do not know if I am even capable of wearing them.
Sansheng said, "Layman, have you not seen Shitou? Can you do it? The layman said, "Picking up one and putting down another—this is not yet the skill of a master hand.

Sansheng said, "This old monk’s affairs as abbot are many. The layman bowed respectfully and departed. Sansheng said, "Picking up one and putting down another—this is indeed the skill of a master hand."
The layman said, "What a fine inquiry into the principle of the One Vehicle! Today, I have lost it. Doushan said, "It is so. It is so.
Thereupon, the layman took his leave of Doushan, who ordered ten Zen practitioners to escort him. Upon reaching the gate, the layman pointed to the snow in the air and said:
"Fine snow, flake by flake, does not fall anywhere else. Zen guest Quan said, "Where does it land? The Master then gave him a slap. Quan said, "You must not be so hasty.
The Master said, "If you call yourself a Zen guest like this, the Old Man Yama will not let you go.
Quan asked, "What about you, Layman? The Master slapped him again and said, "Seeing with one's eyes yet being as if blind; speaking with one's mouth yet—"
He was described as being like one who is mute.
When the layman arrived at Qifeng’s [monastery], as soon as he entered the courtyard, Feng said, "This worldly person enters the monastery so frequently;
what is he looking for? The layman then looked back toward both sides and said, "Who says such a thing? Who says such a thing? Feng then gave a shout. The layman—
The Master said, "Right here. Feng said, "Is this not the Way of the Open Sun? The Layman said, "What about that which is behind you?
Feng turned his head and said, "Look! Look! The Layman said, "The grass-thief is utterly defeated! The grass-thief is utterly defeated!
One day, as Feng was walking alongside the Layman, the Layman took a step forward and said, "I am one step stronger than you, Master. Feng said, "There is no back."
He turned toward the old man, intending to take the lead. The Master said, "The bitterness within bitterness is not yet this one phrase.
Feng said, "I fear the old man will not be satisfied. The Master said, "If the old man cannot endure it, what can you, Feng, possibly endure?
Feng said, "If I had a staff in my hand, I would strike until I was exhausted. The Master then gave him a slap and said, "Not very good. Only then did Feng pick it up.
[Baizhang] raised his staff. The layman seized it and said, "This thief has suffered a total defeat today!
Baizhang laughed and said, "It is my clumsiness; it is your cleverness. The layman then clapped his hands and said, "An equal! An equal!
One day, the layman asked Baizhang again, "How many *li* is it from here to the peak? Baizhang said, "Where have you come from? The layman said, "A truly formidable place."
Jung-yang was stern and rigid; one could not question him further. Feng asked, "How many are there? The scholar said, "One, two, three. Feng said, "Four, five, six.
The scholar said, "Why do you not say seven? Feng said, "As soon as you say seven, there is already eight. The scholar said, "You have stopped me."
Feng said, "Add as much as you wish. The Layman gave a shout and departed; Feng also shouted after him.
One day the Layman asked again, "I cannot speak with such dignity. Feng said, "Bring me back the Master Páng of such a moment.
The Layman said, "Why do you lack spirit? Feng said, "What a fine inquiry! But you have inquired of the wrong person. The Layman said, "A fine arrival! A fine [departure]!"
One day, Chan Master Danxia Tianran came to visit a lay practitioner. As soon as he reached the gate, he saw the woman Lingzhao carrying a vegetable basket.
Danxia asked, "Is the lay practitioner at home? Lingzhao set down the basket and, with palms joined, [stood before him].
As he stood there, Xiang asked, "Is the Layman here? Zhao lifted his basket and walked away. Xiang then departed.

After a short while, the Layman returned. Zhao brought up the previous conversation. The Layman asked, "Is Danxia here? Zhao replied, "He has gone. The Layman said, "It is like applying red earth to a cow's udder.
Xiang followed after him and entered to see the Layman. Upon seeing him coming, the Layman neither rose nor spoke. Xiang then—
Xuan Sha held up his whisk. Xuedou held up his mallet. Xuan Sha said, "Is it merely this, or is there something else?
Xuedou said, "This time seeing you, Master, is not like before. Xuan Sha said, "That will not diminish your reputation. Xuedou said, "I have been intending to strike you for some time.
Xuan Sha said, "In that case, you have silenced the natural mouth. Xuedou said, "Your being silent is due to your own nature."
"Divide it. It makes me dumb as well. Danxia then threw down his whisk and departed. The layman called out, "Wait, Master! Wait, Master! But Danxia paid him no heed.
The layman said, "Not only do you suffer from dumbness, you are further afflicted by deafness. One day, Danxia visited the layman again.
Upon arriving at the gate, they met face to face, and Danxia asked, "Is the Layman at home? The layman replied, "When one is hungry, one does not choose [one's food]."
As they were eating, Lushan Xia asked, "Is Old Pang here? The layman replied, "Heaven! Heaven! and then entered his house.
Lushan Xia said, "Heaven! Heaven! and then turned back. One day Lushan Xia asked the Layman, "How was our meeting yesterday compared to today?

The Layman said, "If you can bring up yesterday's matter according to the Dharma, I will make it into a 'patriarchal eye' (zongyan). Lushan Xia said, "But as for that patriarchal eye, does it still have attachment?"
"Have you attained the state of Master Pang? The scholar said, "I am within your eyes. Yunhua said, "My eyes are narrow;
where can I find a place to settle my body? The scholar said, "How can these eyes be narrow? How can this body be settled? Yunhua withdrew.
The scholar said, "Say one more phrase, and this dialogue will be complete. Yunhua remained silent. The scholar said, "Among all these, this one sentence no one can utter."
He did so. One day, the layman stood with his palms joined before Danxia for a short while and then went out.
Danxia paid him no heed. The layman returned and sat down; Danxia then stood with his palms joined before the layman for a short while and entered the abbot’s quarters. The layman said:
"You enter while I exit; there is still business yet to be settled. Xiang said, "This old fellow enters and exits—when will it ever come to an end?
The Master said, "Yet you lack even a modicum of compassion. Xiang said, "I have led this fellow to such a state."
The scholar said, "What are you holding? Xiang then picked up the scholar's *fuhou* (head-wrap) and said, "This looks like an old master monk.
The scholar then placed the *fuhou* on Xiang’s head and said, "This looks like a young worldly man. Xiang responded with three shouts of "Yes!
The scholar said, "There is still the scent of the past remaining. Xiang then threw down the *fuhou* and said, "It is very much like..."
[Danxia] held up a black silk cap. The Layman then responded with three "yes" sounds. Danxia said, "How can you forget the breaths from days past?
The Layman snapped his fingers three times and said, "It moves heaven and shakes earth. One day, when Danxia saw the Layman coming, he made a gesture of running away.
The Layman said, "That was still a gesture of casting off the body; what about a gesture of groaning and stretching? Danxia then sat down. The Layman then...
Returning to the previous point, [Danxia] used his staff to draw seven characters on the ground. Xiang drew a single character beneath them. The Master said, "Because of the seven, I see the one;
seeing the one, I forget the seven. Danxia said, "Give me a word here. The Master then wept three times and departed.
One day, while the Layman was walking with Danxia, they came upon a pool of water. The Layman pointed at it and said, "Right there—"
"Even so, you still cannot manage it. Xiang said, "Truly, one cannot manage it. The Master then scooped up water and splashed two handfuls onto Xiang.
Xiang said, "Do not do this! Do not do this! The Master said, "It must be done this way! It must be done this way!
Xiang then scooped up water and splashed three handfuls onto the Master, saying, "At this very moment, what can be done? The Master said, "Nothing outside."
Wu said, "Few obtain the advantage. Shushi asked, "Who is it that falls short of the advantage?
One day, Master Bailing encountered a lay practitioner on the road.
Ling asked, "The phrase you found strength in at Mount Nanyue in the past—have you ever brought it up for others? The practitioner replied, "I have brought it up. Ling said, "Bring it up..."

"To whom [are you speaking]? The Master pointed to himself with his hand and said, "Pang Gong. Ling said, "Truly, even Miaode and Śūramgama could not have praised this sufficiently. The Master then asked, "Who knows the phrase by which you attained your power? The Master donned his bamboo hat and walked away. The Master said, "Be careful on your way. Ling did not look back. One day, Ling asked the Layman: [The Layman replied: "I am like a man who has lost his way; I do not know where I am going. Ling said, "If you do not know where you are going, how can you say you have lost your way? The Layman said, "I do not know where I am going, yet I do not know that I have lost my way. Ling said, "If you do not know where you are going, how can you say you do not know that you have lost your way? The Layman said, "I do not know where I am going, nor do I know that I have lost my way. Ling said, "If you do not know where you are going, nor know that you have lost your way, then you are truly a person who has lost their way. The Layman said, "I do not know where I am going, nor do I know that I have lost my way; I simply do not know. Ling said, "If you do not know, how can you say you do not know? Whether you can speak of the Way or cannot, both fail to avoid it. Tell me, first, what is it that they have not avoided? Layman Shi blinked his eyes.
Ling said, "There is nothing more extraordinary than this. Layman Shi said, "Master, you have granted your approval to the wrong person.
Ling said, "Who does not do so? Who does not do so? Layman Shi paid his respects and departed. One day, while Ling was sitting in the abbot’s quarters, Layman Shi entered.
Nan-ch’uan came forward; Ling seized him and said, “The ancients spoke thus; the people of today speak thus. How do you, Layman, speak? The Layman gave Ling a slap.
Ling said, “One cannot help but speak. The Layman said, “To speak is to have a fault. Ling said, “Give me a slap in return.
The Layman stepped forward and said, “Try your hand. Ling then said, “Take care. One day, the Layman asked Pai-ling:
The Master said, "Is this eye capable of sparing people from their mouths? Ling said, "How can it spare them? The Master said, "I knew it; I knew it.
Ling said, "A staff does not strike one who is innocent. The Master turned away and said, "Strike! Strike! Only then did Ling raise his staff.
The Master seized it and said, "Spare me a look. Ling was speechless.
One day, the Layman met Chan Master Datong Puji. Holding up a bamboo sieve in his hand, he said, "Master Datong!
Master Datong! Puji did not respond. The Layman said, "The entire school of Shitou has reached its end at your hands; it has melted away like ice and crumbled like tiles."
Ji said, "If you cannot match Master Pang’s gesture, it is indeed as clear as this. Layman Shi threw down his colander and said, "How could one know it is not worth even a single coin?
Ji said, "Though it is not worth a single coin, how can you avoid owing him? Layman Shi performed a dance and departed.
Ji picked up the colander and said, "Layman! Layman Shi turned his head back; Ji performed a dance and departed. Layman Shi clapped his hands.
Zhizang said, "Go back! Go back! Go back! One day, Linji asked the Layman: "This is a saying that few people from ancient times to the present have been able to avoid with their lips and tongues.
Can you, sir, avoid it? The Layman responded with an affirmative grunt. Linji repeated his previous question.
The layman asked, "Where have you come from? Jie repeated the previous story. The layman asked again, "Where have you come from?
Jie said, "Not only now; the ancients also had such words. The layman performed a dance and departed.
Jie said, "This madman—having gone himself, who else would he have to have inspected? One day, Puji visited a layman. The layman said, "I remember when..."
"When my mother was in her womb, there was a saying that I will cite for you, Master; you must not attempt to analyze it intellectually. Jie said, "That is still from a previous life.
The scholar said, "I told you earlier that you must not analyze it intellectually. Jie said, "This is a startling statement; how could one not be afraid?
The scholar said, "According to your own understanding, Master, yours might be called startling. Jie said, "It is not an intellectual analysis."
Li said, "On the contrary, it becomes a matter of logic. The Master said, "Not only separated by one or two lifetimes.
Ji said, "A monk who eats his rice and gruel may be examined as he pleases. The Master snapped his fingers three times. One day, the Layman went to visit Puzhi.
When Puzhi saw the Layman coming, he immediately shut the door and said, "An old man of much knowledge; do not meet with him. The Layman said, "Sitting alone..."
[The monk] spoke to himself: "Whose fault is this? Jie then opened the door. As soon as he stepped out, the official seized him, saying, "You know much; I know much.
Jie said, "Setting aside 'knowing much' for a moment—how much difference is there between closing a door and opening it, or between rolling up and spreading out [a mat]?
The official said, "Just this one question has exhausted my breath to the point of killing me. Jie remained silent. The official said, "Seeking cleverness, you have only brought about clumsiness."
The Layman went to see Chan Master Changzi. It happened that the Master had ascended the hall and the assembly was gathered in silence.
The Layman stepped forward and said, "Each of you should examine yourselves. Changzi then addressed the assembly. The Layman, however, stood to the right of the meditation seat.

At that time, a monk asked, "Without touching the master of the house, please let the Teacher respond to my question. Changzi said, "Do you recognize Pang Gong? The monk said, "I do not recognize him. The Layman then seized [the monk].
Zhuzi Monastery’s Yunchu said, "Alas! Alas! The monk had no reply. Yunchu pushed him aside and, after a short while, asked the layman, "Did that monk just now receive a beating?
The layman replied, "I shall wait until he is willing before it can happen.

Yunchu said, "The layman sees only the sharpness of the chisel's tip, but does not see the squareness of the chisel's head. The layman said, "If you speak in such a manner, I may well agree with you."
When the outsider heard this, he said, "This is certainly not good. Xizong asked, "What is so bad about it? The scholar said, "Master, you see only that the head of the chisel is square;
you do not see that the point of the awl is sharp."
Once, while drinking tea with the monk Songshan, a layman lifted up his tea bag and asked, "Everyone has their own share;
why then can they not speak? Songshan said, "Precisely because everyone has their own share, they cannot speak.
The layman asked, "Why then can you, my elder brother, speak? Songshan said, "One must not remain without words. The layman said, "Truly so."
"Quite so," said Shanshan as he went to drink tea. The scholar said, "Brother, when you drink tea, why do you not bow to your guest?
Shanshan asked, "Who? The scholar replied, "Pang Gong. Shanshan said, "Why bother to bow?

Later, when Danxia heard of this, he remarked, "Had it not been for Songshan, I might have been deluded by that old fellow for the rest of my life. When the scholar heard this, he sent someone to deliver a message to Danxia.
[The Master] said: "Why did you not grasp it at the moment before the sack was lifted?

One day, while the Layman was looking at a plowing ox with Songshan, the Layman pointed to the ox and said, "In that very moment, it was even more peaceful and happy; it was simply that it did not yet know [itself].
Songshan said, "If it were not for Master Pang, how else would one recognize it? The Layman asked, "Master, what does he not yet know? Songshan—
[The Master] said, "If you have not yet seen Shitou, it does not hinder you from being unable to speak. The Layman asked, "What about after you have seen him?
The Mountain [Master] clapped his hands three times. One day the Layman went to Songshan; seeing the Master carrying a staff, he immediately asked, "What is that in your hand?
The Mountain said, "I am advanced in years; I cannot do without it for even a single step. The Layman said, "Even so..."
His vigor still remained. Deshan struck him. The Master said, "Drop that staff in your hand and bring me a question.
Deshan threw down the staff. The Master said, "This old fellow; his former words do not match his subsequent speech. Deshan then gave a shout.
The Master said, "There is even more grievous suffering than in the blue heavens. One day, while the Layman was walking with Songshan, he saw a monk choosing [his path].
Caishan said, "The yellow leaves are removed; the green leaves remain. The scholar asked, "If they do not fall as yellow leaves, what then? Caishan said, "Speak!
The scholar said, "To act neither as host nor guest is most difficult. Caishan said, "It is precisely because you insist on being the master.
The scholar said, "Who does not do so? Caishan said, "No, no. The scholar said, "In the place where green and yellow do not remain—"
In the midst of this, [Zhaozhou] asked, "Is it possible to go in such a way? The Layman (Shishuang Qingzhu) valued the assembly highly.
[Zhaozhou] said, "The assembly has let you fall into the trap. The Layman then departed.
One day, while Shishuang was conversing with the Layman, he suddenly picked up a ruler on the desk and said, "Do you see this? The Layman replied, "I see it. Shishuang asked, "What do you see?"

The scholar said, "Pine Mountain! Pine Mountain! The mountain man said, "One cannot help but speak. The scholar said, "How could one possibly do so? The mountain man then threw down his measuring rule.
The scholar said, "To have a head but no tail makes one loathed by others. The mountain man said, "It is not you, sir; today you still do not measure up.
The scholar said, "In what way do you not measure up? The mountain man said, "Having a head but no tail. The scholar said, "I have won against such strength."
When it is weak, it exists; when strength is attained within the weak, it is non-existent. Master Shanbao said to the Layman:
"Regarding this old fellow, there is no place for speech therein. The Layman asked Master Benchixi: "In what did Danxia’s intention lie when he struck the attendant?"
Xī said, "An old fellow like me judges others by their strengths and weaknesses. The scholar said, "I would only venture to ask you because we have studied under the same master.
Xī said, "If that is so, bring it up from the beginning and let us deliberate together.
The scholar said, "An old fellow like me must not be allowed to judge right and wrong for you. Xī said, "I take pity on your old age. The scholar said, "My transgression! My transgression!"
One day, when Benchui saw a layman approaching, he gazed at him for a long time. The layman then took his staff and drew a circle on the ground.
Benchui stepped forward and stamped upon it with his foot. The layman asked, "What is this? What is this? Benchui then drew a circle in front of the layman.
The layman also stamped upon it with his foot. Benchui said, "It was there when you came; it is gone now that you leave."
