One must always be wary of the four snakes; hold the mind firm and abandon the three poisons.
When meeting others, discuss the cultivation of the Path; do not further cling to lustful desire. Lustful desire is but a fleeting emotion.

For long kalpas one enters hell; even if one should emerge from there, One will have a strange form unrecognized by others—sometimes becoming four-legged, Or perhaps being entirely footless. It is a pity that this precious human body turns into an ugly-headed beast.
I announce this to you today in advance: in every action, you must exert yourselves with diligence.
My family has long resided on the mountain, having long since departed from the city. Our thatched cottage consists of three rooms:
one room is twelve feet long, one room houses five *ge* (hemp), and one room contains six-four *chen* (dust).
My family lives within these inner rooms; all day long we are idle and have no affairs. Yesterday was the twenty-fifth of the dark fortnight.
In the first watch of the night, drunk with wine, the two men became entangled in confusion.
With all manner of lewd words and provocative airs, they vexed the household beyond endurance. They set fire to the house and its thatched roof;
the five bundles of hemp were reduced to ashes and dust, not even one or two remaining. Everything was swept away and utterly cleansed; only the empty, vacant ground remained.
The self is utterly naked, with no clothing upon the body; do not worry further about thieves, but sleep at ease and in peace.
When equally consumed by the fire, those who have gone forth together abandon afflictions, yet afflictions remain as their companions; with deluded minds, they seek fields of merit.
With a simple mind, I accept deliverance; The twelve links of dependent origination are the governing principle. There is no way to avoid coming and going;
rely on wisdom, not consciousness; Rely on the meaning, not the words.
In the Buddha-mind, the stage of the only child, all that stirs and moves is both male and female; All are equal like empty space, Where neither good nor evil is grasped.
Since no heaven is ever constructed, who would suffer the pains of the three miserable realms? There is a Dharma that exhausts all things without remainder;
by riding upon emptiness, one can deliver oneself. Spirit manifests as the body of the Tathāgata, and wisdom acts as the treasury of the Tathāgata, from which the pāramitās surge forth.
It circulates the path of the True Way; the entire body is nothing but Buddha.
The deluded person does not realize for themselves the eighty secondary marks, nor the thirty-two primary marks;
yet the Four Truths and the Three Vehicles are one and the same in the wisdom of non-arising—this is called the "unified mark. It is not that this person is the same as a skull.
Ordinary beings share the same essence as the Buddha, Their single substance is without distinction.
Yet if one discusses mind and its objects, they are vastly separated and dissimilar: Ordinary beings possess only deluded thoughts;
Grasping at conditions throughout heaven and earth, they constantly harbor the three poisons. Seeking their own benefit by harming others, The Buddha-mind is ever compassionate.
Good and evil are not two; all sentient beings, however they stir, have minds identical to that of an only son.
The six consciousnesses are empty and unarisen; by offering the six sense objects as alms, the faculty of mind becomes wondrous enlightenment—the equalizing wisdom of the seventh consciousness.
The wealthy child walks with empty hands; The poor child carries his own goods.
Dragged by those goods into the marketplace, he cannot leave to buy or sell. When he realizes it is evening, he returns home.
At twilight, all is pitch black; what he seeks does not meet his expectations. The whole family clamors together; He himself lacks the nature of *prajñā*.
Lacking the perfections, one enters the weeds clutching a rope; binding oneself for a hundred years, this is truly pitiable.
In the blinding darkness, one does not see the sun. Though a wealthy man may have empty hands, his home is overflowing with riches;
he possesses an inexhaustible treasury that requires no external objects.
Circulating everywhere, its function is inexhaustible; The essentials emerge from principle. The past was no different from the present;
The present is no different from the past. Life’s affairs perish day by day; there is much one cannot accomplish.
The world lacks wealth and resources; One must guard emptiness, for there are no goods or bribes.

The principles of poetry are renewed day by day; This decaying dwelling grows old moment by moment. Hearing that the boat has not yet been breached by leaks, one must cross the river of craving early;
Having emerged from the confluence of the three rivers, the spirit attains realization in its carefree wandering.
"Reduce it further, reduce it again," And suddenly it becomes a *pātra* tree. As one approaches the path of departure, the road is difficult.
No boat is available to ferry one across; When old karma meets Lord Yama, there is no room for partiality.
If you see the *udumbara* flower, there will be no doubts anywhere.
The worldly masses, in their ignorance, Meet only to discuss money: "Zhang San owes five hundred strings."
Li Si has several thousand [coins], yet Zhao Da loses his principal; Wang Liu suffers misfortune.

His mouth constantly speaks of the three karmas, while the fire of desire burns within his heart. A foolish wolf bites his belly until it is hot, and a greedy ghost seizes his head and drags him along.
Having feet and further legs, he keeps his eyes open yet remains in constant sleep.
The rākṣasas are of one heart; when shall we see the blue sky? The blue sky cannot be seen, for one has formed the karmic conditions for hell.
In one’s own home, one keeps a true wife; one does not delight in seeking external beauty.
A true wife gives birth to sons and daughters; they grow up together, sharing both honor and disgrace. External beauty may also have sons and daughters, [but they are not one's own].
Having grown up, he loves to commit theft; With a wife, he burdens me and comes to me.
He drags me into the prison; I too have known him for long. He lures me into his chamber; inside and out, we are all gathered together.
We eat from a single bowl; once full, we sever all delusions. Where there is no form, there is no merit.
If one discusses the principle of true stillness, all paths lead back to non-attainment. In former days, when I was in the realm of existence, I was constantly deceived by others;
a single mark gave rise to discrimination, and what I saw and heard was full of right and wrong.
Later, having entered the realm of non-existence, I was again deceived by no one; I simply sat, gazing at the mind.
In the profound darkness there is nothing known; To speak of existence or non-existence is equally a clinging.
Where could there be anything? Existence and non-existence are of one essence. All marks are utterly transcended, for the mind is like empty space.
Thus, empty space is my teacher. If one were to discuss the principle of formlessness, Only my father, the King, would know it.
In old age, one lacks the strength to repair the dwelling; The foundation crumbles, pillars rot at their roots, rafters and eaves sag and fall out of place.
The plastered coatings have all fallen away, and the four walls are empty and whistling with the wind.
Lifting my head to look at the beams and columns, I see only scattered white hairs. May the clouds of wisdom descend as the rain of Dharma.
The water of wisdom irrigates the heart’s flow; Within the house, all is spacious and empty. Even if the roof collapses, what cause for grief?
Though the mountain villa and thatched hut fall into ruin, I return to roam within the great mansion. In life after life, I choose no dwelling place;
Following the skull, I preach without seeking. A person has five kinds of flowers; When the flowers wither, they turn into fragrance.
Vaporous clouds fill the old dwelling; offerings are made to one's original father and mother. Someone sees it but does not recognize it, reporting:
"It is the mulberry tree of the tenth month. A single thought of external dust and craving forms a pouch of five colors.
Within the pouch arise three pillars; upon the pillars are a thousand beams. Beside the beams, hell is formed.
Hell becomes heaven because of a band of thieves; They create it themselves and must perish by their own hand.
Even if they were to preserve their lives, When would they ever return to their hometown? Texts speak of concentration and wisdom, yet concentration and wisdom are but father and mother;
Why do you not rely on principle and intellect, But instead pursue sensory forms in a foreign land?
One must soon return to the great mansion, where filial piety allows one to see father and mother.
When father and mother hear that their son has come, they sit upright and greet him with joyful smiles. "I have a treasure storehouse," they say, "entrust you with the key to open it.
Whether one is a poor son or wealthy, the entire nation shall be spared from the three calamities; used as one wishes, it is inexhaustible.
No longer receiving a womb-born body, They roam at ease without obstruction. Day and night they behold the Tathāgata;
The Tathāgata pities all his children, Treating them with equality, without high or low. Yet the children themselves are foolish and deluded, Which makes them difficult to transform and teach.
A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), But the minds of these children have turned treacherous and deceitful.
Send forth your sons to purify the three karmas; turn away from worldly talk and discourses on attachment.
Send forth your sons to cultivate the True within, rather than turning outward to seek the false. Send forth your sons to study formlessness;
grasping at others' marks while holding to non-contention is supreme. Yet when debating principles, they end up cursing one another.
Non-attachment is the supreme gift; non-delusion is the supreme meditation. Non-hatred is the supreme observance of precepts;
mindfulness is the supreme seeking of conditions. To see all things as merely the affairs of ordinary people— When night comes, one sleeps in peace and ease;
In cold weather, one sits by the fire. Yet the fire is fundamentally without smoke; One does not fear the woman of darkness.
Without seeking the Goddess of Merit, Spontaneous skillful means arise; All are like the ship of Prajñā.
If one can train in this way, Merit will truly be boundless.
The ten directions are all equal and one; This is the Temple of Suchness, Within which dwells Amitāyus.
Originally there are no names; ordinary people do not enter into the principle.
Their minds are preoccupied with worldly affairs—begging for money to buy tiles and timber to roof over empty space.
Yet they are driven by the six thieves and turned away from true suchness-wisdom; throughout the day they endure hardship, using deluded thoughts to pursue fame and profit.
A practitioner who trains in this manner will, throughout many kalpas, never arrive at non-existence.
Without retribution, vast and expansive, empty and void, there is nowhere to sit.
Within the house, it is empty, empty, empty, empty—there are no goods. The sun travels within the void; when the sun sets, one lies down within the void.
Sitting in emptiness, chanting poetry in emptiness; Poetry and emptiness harmonize with one another. Do not be surprised that pure emptiness is used;
this is the seat of all Buddhas. Worldly people do not distinguish jewels; Emptiness itself is the true treasure.
If you take offense at the absence of existence, That is simply the fault of the Buddhas.
Some people have what they know; there are matters of right and wrong. Having heard the Way of signlessness, one composes the mind and harbors no doubt.
At five years of age, one does not grow any taller; One remains merely a child, clutching a fist and gnawing at it with the mouth.
For a hundred years, one refuses to let go; Though artificial flowers may be upright and beautiful, [they lack true fragrance].
In the end, it never satisfies hunger; it is all because of foolish children. Not knowing that this is a provisional expedient, they fail to realize the principle of the formless Tathāgata.
All conditioned activity is ultimately non-existent;
where there is anger, there is no need to be angry, and where there is joy, there is no need to be joyful. If one rejoices, lustful desire arises.
Hatred is the arising of a venomous snake; The venomous snake gives rise to a fierce fire. Lust becomes the greedy ghost, and the fierce fire unites with the greedy ghost;
Ignorance is a wolf that stifles the mind’s foundation. Delusive thoughts are like the sands of the Ganges;
afflictions have no end. Nescience is pitch-black darkness; When thirst comes, one drinks only brine.
All day long you run about on account of worldly affairs, Refusing to enter the principle of emptiness;
You cherish the view of self like a beast, Knowing yourself to be a mere wretch. You pervert the law to take money from others, Boasting that you are skilled at calculation;
Once you have acquired it, the whole family uses it, Yet when suffering arrives, there is no one to accompany you.
Though powerful, one must endure being ridden by others; A staff and whip are driven upon the back.
A leather headpiece is placed upon the snout, and an iron plate is held in the mouth; The neck is worn through, and the nostrils are bound with a sharp cord.
One reaps what one has sown; Even a Buddha cannot sever this.
The foolish child lacks wisdom; He despises his own father for being ugly.
Born from his mother’s body, he despises her for lacking beauty; He abandons his own parents And wanders abroad chasing after sensual forms.
He treats his six kin as mere acquaintances, Never ceasing his idle chatter, Constantly roaming through the twelve months.
Month after month he drinks the wine of lust, Night after night he never awakens from his stupor.
A drunken man who vomits his filth to feed pigs and dogs— Such a wretched man!
Because of this unfinished business, I possess a precious sword, Not made of the iron of this world; Once forged, it requires no further sharpening.
Crystal clear and white as snow, its vapor surges and disperses floating clouds; its light shines through the three thousandfold world-system.
It roars with the sound of a lion, causing the brains of all beasts to split. All foreign lands submit in surrender, and sentient beings are entirely extinguished.
Having been extinguished, they are born again; being born again, they become golden locks (guxue).
Carrying [it] along, one travels everywhere; to those who find joy, one explains it as such.
Know that I am turning the Prajñā; see me turning the Vajra. With palms joined in reverent prostration, remaining utterly unmoving, one beholds the King of Emptiness.
This is superior even to giving away one’s body and life; it is also superior to dwelling in the heavenly realms.
It surpasses making offerings at Mount Wutai; it surpasses seeking rebirth in the Western Paradise. To abide without abiding—its merit is immeasurable.
Conditioned things are like dreams and illusions; the signless accords with the true permanence.
Through the Tathāgata’s great compassion, he extensively expounds the pāramitās and fully understands the suffering of the three realms.
I earnestly urge you to go forth; yet having attained it, you are unwilling to practice. You are truly a stubborn and callous being.
He has already become a Buddha; you are one who shall become a Buddha. That you shall attain it but do not—whose fault is this?
Do not blame the Buddhas of the past for the suffering that will follow you through future kalpas.
Whose son is this noble sir? Opening his eyes, he creates hell. He perverts the law to take people’s money to support that pack of thieves.
Though his household may be great, once karma is formed, there is no escape.
Only when the cycle of rebirth is complete can one change form to repay the debt. Look at the donkey you ride!
Always appearing thus in form, One is needlessly beaten with whips and staves. Though one has reason, it cannot be explained;
The fool breaks the jar. Seeking protection from others, One obtains wealth through evil means.
Intending to offer alms to repair the breach, The nature of the object does not correspond; There is no need to labor over this matter.
Even if one possesses a small amount of merit, how could that lead to hell?
When will sin and merit meet head-on? If one’s own root is already severed, how can there be a favorable path?
First, one must uphold the five precepts before one can obtain a human body; having wealth, one should practice giving.
If one practices the ten wholesome deeds, the body shall never suffer from poverty. Hearing the Way brings the blessings of gods and humans;
yet the birth and death of gods and humans come and go like the wheels of a cart. Even reaching the Brahma world through conditioned effort does not equal a single hair’s breadth of the True.
Should you wish further to discuss the profound and mysterious, I fear the Dharma King might be displeased.
Comparing one hide with another hide, The grandson is not equal to the son. Sitting in meditation is superior to reading scriptures;
Reading scriptures is superior to conditioned activities. Seeking the words without knowing the principle— Abandoning the mother to nourish the aunt;
The aunt is the physical body, The mother is the Dharma-body; The physical body is but mere letters.
The Dharma-realm is the unconditioned principle; Letters and words arise and perish. Yet the signless remains perfectly as it is.
The Buddha’s teaching is fundamentally without falsehood; Every word must be discussed in terms of reality.
To discipline oneself and benefit others— This is what is called "hidden virtue" (yinze) in the secular world. Whether one be a Heavenly King, Or even a Prime Minister or a nephew—none are exempt.
In this world there are the noble and the lowly, yet by the power of karma they are all one and the same. I tell you, O wealthy man:
do not treat the poor child with contempt. It is through the force of accumulated heavy karma that one’s state is formed; once overturned, it is difficult to escape.
Regretting only your own delusion, when something happens you have no one to know of it, and you lie there stretching out your two legs in vain sleep.
At dawn, he did not reflect: "The Buddhas are my fathers; I am the Son of the World-Honored One.
Now that I have grown to maturity, I shall act as a guide in place of my father. Father and son dwell in the same house, never parting for even a single step.
The Dharma-body has no form or appearance; how could the people of the world ever know it?
This pack of thieves has, life after life, deceived their master. Now that I have recognized you, I shall no longer associate with you.
If you do not submit to me, I will speak of you everywhere so that all people recognize you, cutting off your path for travel. But if you can submit to me, [I shall treat you differently].
I do not discriminate, nor do I consider myself one and the same as you. Forever free from birth and death, I am unlike those worldly people who prize jewels.
My fame brings me contentment; my heart does not dwell on wealth and status.
I find joy only in the simple meal of a single bowl; I have no desire for the mirror of grooming or the scales of office.
When hungry, eat the rice of the western mountains; when thirsty, drink from the source spring.
In the cold, don the robe of formlessness; when heat comes, sleep beneath the pines. Knowing that this body has no ultimate reality, let the remaining years pass spontaneously.
The mist is heavy and the sun finds it hard to emerge; the clouds are thick and the moon is dim. If you have a mind that seeks to find the Buddha, [you will never see him].
Day and night you apply your mind to practice, yet the words spoken in dreams are not yet realized. Hearing the truth, your ears become deaf;
when the bandits sit across the road, how can the Way be passed? If your realization of nature were truly lucid, there would be no need for much seeking or explanation.
To grasp the words of ordinary people and sages is, in the end, nothing but emptiness.
How does he expound for the sake of others? He teaches the suchness that is free from marks. The mind-mirror is both empty and still; there is neither reality nor unreality.
The mind’s function is eternally silent yet active. Transcending the world, he enters the remainderless [nirvana];
Brahmā, Śakra, and all others pay him homage. Bodhisattvas likewise dwell with him. His speech is the speech of ordinary beings.
This is a letter in accord with the principle of Śākyamuni. If one can study in this manner, one will not labor in vain.
At dawn I drink thin gruel; after the meal, I gather two bundles of firewood.
Having sold them for two sheng of rice, it suffices to support my remaining body. With no hunger-fire to oppress me, I bring peace to my formless spirit.
The divine spirit dwells in peace within the pure Buddha-land; Inwardly and outwardly, all dust and defilement are severed.
Without interval, one preaches Prajñā, opening wide the gates and ferries. Though fire consumes all household possessions, One becomes a person entirely free from worldly concerns.
The perfect mirror is as bright as the sun, Surging forth unimpeded wisdom— In the Sanskrit tongue, this is called *pāramitā*.
In the language of Tang, this means "The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings. The speaker speaks of signlessness;
The one who departs departs from words and letters, Speaking only of the Unsurpassed Way. Benefiting others is itself self-benefit.

If one can enter into the practice of principle, remaining unshakable like the earth, One will not be constantly preoccupied with worldly affairs; It would be better than merely stretching out one's legs to sleep.
I observe those within the three realms who dwell in thatched huts; Snakes and rats share the same burrow, and by day it is always as if night.
Pigeons act as kinsmen, and rākṣasas converse with hearts in accord;
Five dogs constantly howl and bark—contemplating this makes one fearful. I observe that all of this is but an illusion.
The name "empty space" is also provisional; Like a cowherd’s grass hut where cattle graze, The three bodies are a single transformation.
The Tathāgata’s one true wisdom Pervades the Sahā world-system. Though he diligently explains expedient means, Some people do not understand them for themselves.
There is nowhere that the mind does not arise; In many places, there is much greed and attachment.
The mind-king commits black karma, yet instructs others to repent with their mouths; the mouth repents while the mind does not change—mind and mouth are in opposition.
Not taking the medicine of no-mind, the root of the illness will never be cured.
Clinging to signs to seek Bodhi, one cannot avoid returning the debt.
On Fragrant Mountain there is sandalwood; on Jewel Mountain there is no *eranda*.

When the Golden Mountain illuminates a single hair-tip, that hair-tip becomes ten billion times vast. Sitting in an empty room with a pure mind, Wondrous Virtue is securely established in the four directions.
Ākāśagarbha knows both the internal and external, and entrusts these matters to Ānanda. If one can penetrate this principle—
Non-abiding is nirvana;
if you can employ the words of the sign, I shall teach you a single secret: grasp the arrows of the three poisons and bend them all at once.
The field becomes the four emptinesses, and the five dog-teeth are all broken off.
The aggregate of form perishes of its own accord, and the six thieves are all extinguished.
Yama becomes the Dharma King, and the rākṣasas become bodhisattvas. Let alone one’s own body—the entire nation rejoices at once.
When people realize this is an illusion, even if their hearts are harmed, they remain as such; even the devas cannot escape hardship.
How much more so for this Jambudvīpa— One must seek the unsurpassed principle; Do not further linger in hardship.
When food and clothing are merely sufficient, There is no need to accumulate surpluses. Having few desires leads to Nirvana; Contentment is not the mark of an ordinary person.
In the future there will be no hells; In the present one escapes the three miserable realms.
If one externally severs all攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective attachments), joy will constantly manifest before one.
What was originally obtained? Auspiciousness manifests its own form. Born from emptiness, he is called the Elder; Dipamkara always illuminates him.
Maitreya is his fellow student; Śākyamuni is his elder brother. They sit in succession according to their supernormal powers.
There is no need to laboriously inquire after names or surnames; though names and forms have distinctions, the Dharma-body is of one and the same form.
The meaning of the Mahāyāna is uniform and equal: it is fundamentally without obstruction or closure.
Ordinary beings, clinging to marks, seek with their minds and thus give rise to attachments; when there is no mind, this is true emptiness, and emptiness-quiescence is the fundamental essence.
Neither questioning nor speaking, Constantly illuminating, never allowing it to cease. The Buddha’s heirs, having practiced the Way, No longer grieve over coming or going.
In the pure and cool temple of non-thought, The aggregates are empty; this is the true Mount Wutai. Facing objects, the mind remains undefiled.
When the mind of emotion has died out like cold ashes, the wondrous principle manifests therein; the udumbara flower blooms within the void.

Seek not the truth through seeking, but let the eye of Dharma be true; leave behind appearances to see the Tathāgata. If one can train in this way, they will remain unmoving and escape the three calamities.
I have often heard of the Buddha Akṣobhya, Whom I intended to seek in the eastern direction.
Today, through careful reflection, I see that he is immovable and has arrived naturally. I say to you, my gatekeeper slave: why must you trouble me so?
I shall report this to my father the King; I will change your name for you, And destroy your conditioned achievements.
Revealing the unconditioned path, one knows the joy of sentient beings’ happiness; Driven by the rope of conditions, they wander in delusion.
The wisdom-joy of Bodhisattvas has neither rope nor bondage. If there are those who resolve their minds [on enlightenment], They must directly study non-action.
Do not say you fear falling into emptiness; even attaining emptiness is not bad. Seeing ore but failing to distinguish the gold, one enters the mine only to realize the error.
Suffering and pain exhaust the body and mind; one tires the spirit seeking official rank, only to briefly don the robes of worldly status.
Striking with his hands, he assumes an expression of rage; With every word he utters, he beats the slave-soldiers. With every sound, he commands them to pull out their ribs.

Hearing that they are being sent off for the old king, Even if their limbs were curved, they are made straight. Even if one possesses reason, even if one tries to explain the circumstances, it is of no avail.
When the head of the household drinks wine, the entire family becomes intoxicated at once; A fire breaks out and burns the old residence, yet water is carried to douse an empty plot of land;
Fire and water erupt simultaneously from above one's head, and the three calamities arise all at once.
Doves and pigeons dance in the sky, while a mule arrives to assist by letting out flatulence; Within the causal conditions, there is no fine flower.

The result is that those who lose their way on the path of the Way of Heavenly Principle are truly pitiable; they are entangled by the delusions of thieves, and evil conditions are bestowed upon them at every turn.
There is a Dharma that pervades the Sahā world—open your eyes and behold the Buddha’s words!
Washing the tongue to read the scriptures, harmonizing with the sutras while playing with snakes and mice; when a thought stirs, the three realms become lost and confused.
At that moment, the body manifests the affairs of an ordinary person, yet when one looks inward, it is clearly manifest within the trichiliocosm.
All sentient beings filling the world-systems, In a single instant, create the karma of existence;

To clearly and fully know that they are all contained within a single mustard seed— This is called the *Nirākāra-sūtra* (The Sutra of Formlessness). Those who constantly uphold it do not recognize it;
when one recollects it, there is neither form nor sound.
Studying the Buddha is a matter of dreaming; there is no need to discuss hells. One completely transcends paradise, and the six consciousnesses become one’s servants.
When mind after mind abides nowhere, dust does not adhere in any place.
When the passage through the five realms of existence is cut off, this mindlessness is the ultimate bliss—like seeing the udumbara flower in the void.
Sentient beings build bridges and fords desiring to attain Buddhahood swiftly; They study only the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
By constantly examining the mind with effort, afflictions are exhausted at that moment; The door to the treasury of the seven jewels opens, And wisdom becomes inexhaustible.
Extensively expound the pāramitās; have no mind for stinginess or parsimony. I only fear that people are attached to existence and, being deluded, do not believe themselves.
The world is clever on the surface of the skin, but in their hearts they are headstrongly deluded; others covet the benefits before their eyes.
Who knows that after this, you will not be deceived by the barbarians? Boasting that your hands and feet are slow, you run to see Old Yama;
Dragging a rice-pounder backward, I fear you have not yet awakened.
Today I report this to you for your knowledge.
Those of middle capacity delight in tranquility; those of inferior capacity prefer outward decorum.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is unimpeded, yet it is like that of ordinary people, whom the ordinary do not recognize. The Buddha is the essence of formlessness; why must one rely on forms?
It suffices that the mind understands the matter; let outsiders doubt as they may. It is like a person who drinks water when thirsty.
When cold and heat are known by the mind itself and it does not receive sensory objects, the mind will not become deranged.
With wondrous wisdom acting as the master of the mind, one is called the King who Destroys Existence; in an instant, one realizes the six perfections and employs the five kinds of incense.
This is the true Ultimate Bliss, And this is also the true Western Land. Śākyamuni and Amitāyus dwell together in this site of enlightenment;
Without abandoning worldly affairs, One secretly conceals the study of desire within, While gaining a false reputation for fame in the world.

Transcending all, remain unattached; let thoughts cease as the three realms are seen as empty. Without seeking liberation from the five turbidities, the Dharma-body and Reward-body are both perfected;
the faculty of mind achieves perfect enlightenment. If one can cultivate in this way, even the status of a Wheel-Turning King is not worth a fraction of it.
If the five aggregates were truly existent, they would possess form and shape; If the five aggregates were truly non-existent, they would likewise lack form and sound.
They exist merely as provisional names, which is why delusions come to abide therein.
If one realizes that names and appearances are empty, all phenomena will be exhausted and total clarity will arise; The sovereign mind-king will then be free from all obstruction.

Transcending the activities of the three realms, I am a body of an ordinary being; Delighting in expounding the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), My nature is free from stinginess and greed, and I constantly practice impartial giving.
Ordinary beings engage in conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), But Buddha-wisdom transcends birth and death.
Whether becoming a Buddha or an ordinary person, everything is entirely up to you.
With the ears, hear the principle of formlessness; with the eyes, remain empty and do not receive forms. With the nose, smell the fragrance of formlessness;
with the tongue, taste food that is without form. With the body, wear garments of formlessness; with the mind, follow the attainment of formlessness.
With a tranquil mind, one transcends all devas; with a pure spirit, one beholds Maitreya. Throughout the ten directions, the One Vehicle is uniform;
without discriminating between north and south, he compassionately preaches this Dharma. He manifests illness for the sake of sentient beings, as Cunda offers his final offering.
Wondrous Virtue likewise acts in concert; though names and appearances differ, the Dharma-body is of one form, while emanations number in the thousands of millions.
Only then is the name "Emptiness" established; there is no need to cling to the existence of dharmas—this is the greatest essence of perfect penetration.
If you wish to attain true Buddhahood, have no mind toward the myriad things. When the mind is as it is and the environment is likewise, true wisdom emerges from suchness.
Adorned equally with meditative concentration and wisdom, extensively expound the *pāramitās* so they may circulate throughout the ten directions.
None of those who possess [obstructions] can proceed swiftly; thus I report this to you, O seeker of the Way.
To become a Buddha simply by this means—reading scriptures requires understanding their meaning. Only by understanding the meaning does one begin to practice;
if one can study according to the meaning, one enters the City of Nirvana. To read scriptures without understanding their meaning is, for the most part, no different from being blind.
Though the written texts occupy a vast space, you are unwilling to plow within your own mind. Field after field is nothing but weeds;
from where, then, shall the rice grow?
If someone cannot explain this, it is because their sovereign mind is dark, unable to settle its own affairs.
A band of thieves is buried within; These many thieves are full of greed and delusion. Driven by circumstances, they engage in right and wrong;
The King of the Mind is made their servant. From kalpa to kalpa there is no time of escape; One sees the flower but does not know the tree— Only when the fruit ripens shall one finally understand.
Your family dwells in the village, while I myself reside in the mountain valleys. The mountains are empty and possess nothing;
the village has a hundred kinds of things. Those who have eat their food; those who have not merely open their mouths wide.
The mouth is empty and the belly is also empty; they take that emptiness to consume what exists. When existence is exhausted, all things return to emptiness.
The Buddhas of the three times and all sentient beings are of one essence; from the beginning, we have been of one and the same family.
Failing to recognize our own true kin, we look outward to acknowledge false fathers. We refuse to pluck the udumbara flower, instead gathering only the gourd blossoms.
Before the gourd flowers have fallen, they are constantly plucked by three or five; such as these, they revolve through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
I was once a rustic farmer, the poorest man in the world; there was not a single thing in my home.
Opening their mouths, they speak of emptiness and further emptiness; those former evil associates have all been ordained as monks and sit together in harmony.
They constantly teach others to listen to the Mahāyāna; at mealtime, they hold out their bowls, and I alone provide for them.
Equal and without duality, dwelling together in the same abode all day long; Yet worldly people do not understand, and with deluded minds they give rise to external conditions and grasping.
Having grasped external forms as "Buddhas," their pleasure turns instead into suffering, and from that suffering, all phenomena arise.
By what means can one cross the great ocean? This is to repay those who understand my intent.
While you look well upon the road, there is a precious jewel in your own ancestral home; instead, you seek it in the fields and wilds.
This pack of thieves deceives you, leaving you in vain toil. It is like applying makeup to mud, or smearing oil on a wall.
The fool sees dream-phenomena, yet praises the path he can cultivate; on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, there is not a single thing to be gathered.
Having lost his mind in the mountains, he speaks with spontaneous ease; as soon as he speaks, it is the state of emptiness.
In the void there are no snakes or mice; when the mind exists, waves arise. When there is no mind, this is the Pure Land;
from the Pure Land, the True Buddha is born. The Buddha transmits the Buddha’s words; the Buddha can deliver sentient beings, for sentient beings are the Mother of the Buddha.
The mind-king cannot comprehend it; why not rely on true wisdom? With a single roar, the hundred beasts are subdued, and all see the principle of non-birth.
The principle of non-birth is exceedingly vast. Without mind, there is nothing to be seen—neither internal, nor external, nor in between.
It is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana. All dharmas have no place of abiding.
Wandering at ease, the spirit is naturally at peace;
seeking elsewhere is not the true treasure. Non-thought is the jewel within one's own house. To seek the Buddha-dharma outside the mind is always to walk the path of inversion.
Even the name "Prajñā" is but a provisional designation; how could one rely further upon the written word?
All that has form is empty and false; That which is formless is truly real.
In daily activities there is no distinction; Only I am in spontaneous accord with them. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting;
In every place, do not allow discordance to arise. Who assigns the titles "red" or "purple"? The green mountains are utterly free from dust.
Supernatural powers and wondrous functions—carrying water and hauling firewood—are all such things.
The faculty of mind has no inherent nature; all phenomena are originally void. External objects do not exist at all;
the three realms are naturally non-existent. Where now are the five aggregates? They have all entered the realm of Nirvana without remainder.
The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all contained within a single hair-pore;
yet names and forms are fundamentally non-existent. For those deluded ones who desire [the truth], one must provisionally preach it when the time is right.
The afflictions of delusion must be eliminated; in Prajñā there is neither right nor wrong, neither reality nor falsehood.
The eighty-four thousand fascicles ultimately all return to the same suchness.
If a person possesses even a single fascicle of scripture— which is signless and nameless— there is no one who can recite it, and there is no "I" who can hear it.
If one is able to recite it, one will attain entry into principle and accord with the non-arising of dharmas.
Not debating the Bodhisattva path, the Buddha did not toil to achieve it;
the Father sits upon the throne, and the Son stands before him. Father and son dwell in the same house, so that the minor demons dare not enter.
At that time, he opens the inexhaustible treasury, providing for those who are poor.
Having attained it, one is forever inexhaustible; One escapes the arising of sorrow and anxiety.
If you wish to obtain the true *amṛta*, The three poisons must be removed. Without the scent of ghee or curd, You will spontaneously behold the wish-fulfilling jewel.
It cannot be burned even by the kalpa-ending fire, And it floats amidst the waves of the ocean.
Those who once coerced you with force are today your slaves.
To report this to you so you may seek the True Principle: you have lived a stolen life, feigning deafness.
When your life and body come to an end, your mind and mouth fall into confusion; you cannot give away your own life, yet you would hire others for money.
To read the Tathāgata’s teaching, to rescue and protect the tens of thousands of households within my spiritual city— I am unable to endure my constant solitude.
From time to time, when the lions roar, the birds and beasts all perish; he taught me to become Rāhula, leaving no trace while upholding the precepts and discipline.
Simply knowing how to enter the principle and sit—
this is from the *Collected Poems of Layman Pang*,
Volume Lower, regarding the poem "The Sun Rises at Guduk."
The skulls of sentient beings are of many varieties, yet the Buddhas are all of one kind.
When a commoner beholds a Son of Heaven, he knows how many layers of barriers separate them; yet if there were a whip that transcends men, desiring to see [the Buddha] would not be difficult.
If within that whip one accords with the sacred principle, one may sit and take the office of the state.

The Perfection of Wisdom is from the beginning suchness; When the illnesses of sentient beings are entirely removed, Furthermore, through this perfection one protects the Dharma, entering all things without exception.
All Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Were identical in this single path.
If one can penetrate this principle, An ordinary person is no longer an ordinary person.
The four great elements are fundamentally insentient; Pure and void, they lack form or sound.

The person of realization understands the principle of emptiness, Knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn. All Buddhas are ever present before them; Sublime virtue likewise acts in concert.
In non-existence there is no obstruction; Yet the ox of the mind refuses to plow.
Dust calls before the six gates; the insentient do not enter when called. Both of them are entirely empty; naturally the lips do not get wet.
From this point on, causes and conditions are severed. Ge-wu follows conditions and emerges;
there is only the house of empty stillness. Yuan-ba is identical to Jin-qi.

Entering into principle is like shooting an arrow; Seeking through the words, one turns away from it. Refusing to walk the direct path, one follows the tracks of consciousness and falls into deluded retreat.
The Sovereign Mind does not understand its own affairs, And the official ministers give rise to grasping and obstruction;
Because of this pack of thieves, Birth and death are like treading a water mill.
When another intends to strike you, withdraw your foot as soon as it touches the ground.
Should we meet again in the future, they will be ashamed, yet I shall not be. Patience is the supreme path; throughout kalpas there has been no enmity.
This is the realm of non-arising; it does not belong to the continent of Nirvana.
Abusing others brings no benefit; one should not seek security through such means. When there is no anger, the spirit is naturally at peace;
by abusing others, one only harms oneself. By practicing patience, one gains the merit of the Dharma; by abusing others, one merely incurs loss. Anger and joy are of the same suchness;
thus, one may withdraw from the world without becoming despondent.
Those who understand karma are few; those lost on the path are many. Amidst suffering, they conceive the notion of pleasure;
devoid of joy, they force themselves to sing and play music. They do not drink, yet they seek ordinary intoxication; In a state of stupor, they drown in the river of craving.
Smiling as they create calamity and fault, Their future suffering cannot be avoided by others.
When hearing others' insults with one's ears, know them in the mind but do not respond with words.
Dislike the evil, yet do not crave the good. Be expansive and open, free from the barriers of the mundane world.
Like space, there is no obstruction—this is the Truly Immovable Buddha, also named Avalokiteśvara.
The upturned palm is heaven; the overturned palm is hell. Neither hell nor heaven does my mind belong to.
Even when the illusory city has not yet been left behind, how much more so for the blessings of the various heavens—seeking none of them at all, vast and empty, there is nothing to be attained.
The Buddha possesses a singular compassion; Some people do not understand this mind. All are equal;
He pities both the poor and the wealthy alike. O wealthy ones, do not be greedy; O poor ones, do not be deluded.
Without greed, the mind is naturally still; Without delusion, the intellect has nothing to dwell upon.
The white-robed do not grasp at signs; true principle arises from emptiness.
It is precisely because the mind is unimpeded that wisdom emerges in all directions. There is only the lion’s roar; the jackal’s howl is not permitted.
Awakening is called most wondrous, yet even this is rebuked as a mere provisional name.
If one eradicates from the root, it is severed; if one cultivates from the root, it is extinguished. If one can sever both stumps, the three vehicles are completely transcended.
This is not the speech of an ordinary person, but is clearly explained by the Wondrous Auspicious One (Mañjuśrī) as the healing treatment of the Tathāgata. Once corrected, it shall never recur.
Having long planted the roots of goodness, though amidst the dust of the world, the dust does not invade; it is not that the dust fails to stain, but rather that I am naturally without mind.
With no-mind, the mind does not arise; transcending the three and surpassing the ten stages, one reaches the ultimate fruit of true suchness—when all is said and done, it is simply this.
The wisdom of ordinary beings is narrow in scope; They falsely speak of difficulty and ease.
Free from marks like space, they fully accord with the wisdom of all Buddhas; The marks of precepts are like space. Deluded people create for themselves the root of illness through grasping;
They refuse to pull it out, clinging to these as if playing with flower branches.
Oxherd drives the empty chariot, together entering the dwelling of non-action. The dwelling of non-action is exceedingly vast;
sentient beings, however, find it narrow. The ten directions are one single room; how could there ever be any separation?
Those with the Dharma-person do not grasp; those without mind naturally cross over calamity.
The supreme matter in the world is none other than the power of cultivating the Way.
If one awakens to the principle of non-arising, the three realms will naturally vanish. When the aggregates are empty, wondrous virtue manifests;
this absence of thought is the cool clarity—this is the land of Amitābha. Where else would one seek the Western Paradise?
A precious jewel was tied within my inner garment for immeasurable time;
Yet meeting six evil associates, they constantly feigned compassion, Leading me to drink the wine of desire. Intoxicated, I lay down, utterly unaware that my wisdom was exhausted;
When the wine was finished and I awoke, I beheld my original Teacher once more.
The people of the world prize rare treasures, But I value the stillness of a single moment. Much gold disturbs the human mind;
in stillness, one perceives the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). When this nature is empty, all phenomena (*dharma*) are also empty. The eighteen realms are cut off from their tracks;
If only one’s own mind is free from obstruction, Why worry that the spirit will not penetrate?
Sitting upright, one seeks that which accords with the Dharma; yet that which accords with the Dharma is itself contrary [to seeking].
Casting aside the Dharma, without a mind to grasp, only then does one return to the source. Without seeking, there is no exit from the three realms; to have thoughts is to fall into delusion.
To seek a Buddha or search for liberation is not the way of a true man.
Evil thoughts fill the three realms; though the mouth recites Amitābha’s name, the heart and mouth are at odds.
As a swarm of bandits multiplies, a single speck of dust gives rise to ten thousand objects, suddenly pervading the Sahā world.
Seeking the Buddha-way through form and sound, one ends up as nothing but a demon.
The myriad dharmas arise from the mind; When the mind arises, the myriad dharmas arise.
Once these dharmas have arisen, there is the realization of coming and going as a futile wandering. I address those who cultivate the Way: Do not give rise to existence within emptiness.
If you can penetrate this principle, You will emerge unshakably from the deep pit.
The Buddha is not separate from the mind, and the mind is not separate from the Buddha. When the mind is quiescent, that is bodhi;
when the mind is active, it becomes a thing. When there is a thing, it turns into a demon; when there is nothing, there are no Buddhas.
If one can practice in this way, how could the eighteen [dhātus] arise?
The sheep-cart entices the lowest of fools; The deer-cart carries those of middling capacity; The Great Vehicle is for the superior man.
A phoenix’s nest is not the dwelling of a crane; A *jiaoliao* bird dwells on the eye of a mosquito. O Layman, shame on you, blind donkey!
If one discusses the substance of the *Indra-jāla* net, Ultimately, there is but the One Vehicle.
Some people detest Old Pang; Old Pang does not detest them. He opens his door to wait for those who know him, yet those who know him do not come to visit.
If the mind possesses the Three Studies, then sensory dust and consciousness will not be in discord.
One elixir cures ten thousand ailments; there is no need for many prescriptions and remedies.
The vast and boundless waters of the Yangtze River flow on, circling back to begin again. So too is the cycle of rebirth for the bewildered beings of the three realms.
In this cycle, one changes form and appearance, yet the color of the Yangtze remains unchanged.
To alter one’s appearance exhausts the spirit and consciousness; yet in the end, one must surely reach the ground of Buddhahood.
When sleepy, one stretches out the legs and sleeps; when the principle is realized, one rises to compose a poem.
Within this poem there is no other intent than to exhort the breaking of greed and delusion. When greed, anger, and delusion are exhausted, one is truly a son of the World-Honored One.
There is no need to trouble the master; the King of the Mind should know this for itself.
The people of the world prize fame and profit, but my mind is entirely otherwise. I bundle firewood for sale and trade a pint of rice;
I boil it in a clean iron cauldron. When I perceive it is cooked, I lift the cauldron down; bringing it close to my side, I drop it into my mouth from time to time.
My belly is full, and my stomach remains silent.
To practice and study that which is not the true Way is but to exhaust one’s spirit and body in vain;
to seek the moon’s reflection for a thousand miles is ultimately a labor of futility. Failing to realize that it arises from sound and form, those who study today are but negligent;
simply observe the place where arising and ceasing occur—this is True Suchness.
I shall teach you the method for slaying the thief: Do not employ many arduous means. With the sword of wisdom, pierce the heart;
when the mind perishes, the dharmas perish. When the mind perishes, one reaches the Land of Ultimate Bliss; when the dharmas perish, that is the Western Paradise.
The thief becomes the elephant and horse; the spirit itself becomes the King of Emptiness.
Do not laboriously seek great learning; look instead at that Superior Person. The hundred kalpas and the sun and moon are fundamentally within a single hair-tip and speck of dust.
When the mind is simply tranquil and signless, one immediately crosses the ford of ignorance.
If one can train in this way, how much mental energy will be spared!
The King of Good Intentions, possessed of shame and remorse, Is born within the Hall of the Lotus.

He constantly wields the sword of Prajñā, And throughout the day carries the life-preserving float. Ever cherishing the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha), The five hundred sons of the elders, Relying upon his gracious light, Follow him together back to their native land.
With a sense of shame and a virtuous mind, There is neither self nor other;
Without a stained self and without the defilements of others added, One always dwells in the ground of purity.
Knowing that one cannot surpass existence, One leaves behind former evil associates; Seeing all as Amitābha.
With a sense of shame and integrity and a fine faculty of speech, you constantly open the gate of the Great Way.
The reality of the three realms of existence in this world cannot be discussed; when meeting others, speak only of the Way. Do not further engage in inquiries of health or greetings;
clearly knowing that worldly phenomena are illusory, conventional etiquette is but a needless trouble.
The pair of shame and remorse alone—constantly contemplate the sound of liberation. If one speaks of worldly chatter, truly it cannot be heard;
hearing of wealth, the ear does not admit it; hearing of form, the mind does not give rise to it.
Not accepting talk of existence or non-existence, why worry about not being alert?
The pair of eyes of shame and remorse have seen many kinds of people; they neither love the handsome nor resent the ugly.
Even if one were as beautiful as a celestial maiden, what need is there to give rise to delusive dust?
Lowering one's head to examine one's own form, not a single part is true; body and mind are like illusions and transformations.
Filling the eyes, there is neither enemy nor kin;
shame and modesty are but a single body. In the Brahma-language it is called Vārāṇasī.
Beset by a band of thieves, one is rendered constantly lacking in self-mastery. It is also named "The Dry Well," and it is also named "The Leather Bag."
It is also called the Decayed Old House; It is also called the Illusion Samādhi.
The Buddha rebuked him for being a corpse, yet he rode upon a corpse across the great ocean. The great ocean originally has no water; The corpse is not a boat.
If one examines the affairs of the world with discernment, They are all but false causes and conditions. If one thoroughly understands the characteristics of body and mind, [One realizes this truth.]
Lying across at will in the midst of emptiness, Possessing these six forms of shame and remorse, Truly one does not seek heaven;
from moment to moment, One moves forward step by step. Impermanence has its limits, yet one knows not when it will come— Morning or evening.
When the ancients spoke but a single word, They prepared in advance for the child who dies in poverty.
Hearing this, practice the Way for a short while; do not wait until the time of old age and decay.
When the omen of death suddenly arrives, it will surely deceive you—of this have no doubt. I urge you, but you are unwilling to listen. The three miserable realms are truly pitiable.
Day after day passes, and the hundred years of life gradually come to an end; quickly eliminate deluded thoughts!
Non-thought realizes the true Buddha; do not further strain yourself in pursuit of external conditions.
Gazing upon the things of this world, you suddenly find impermanence has arrived.
Though you have struggled for eons, you cannot escape; night after night, the passage of time grows ever more brief. I tell you, O King of the Mind: this is the Way.
Rely on wisdom, do not rely on consciousness; by relying on wisdom, one sees the true Buddha. By relying on consciousness, one enters hell;
if one sinks into the six realms of existence, there is no time when suffering ends.
Year after year, one’s efforts serve only to prolong the delay, as the skin wrinkles because the flesh diminishes.
The hair is white and the marrow withered; the pores are permeable to the wind. The bones have wasted away, leaving the rafters and eaves exposed;
with scant water, one cannot endure the heat; with little fire, one cannot endure the cold. This illusory body is like a mass of foam; the four elements are likewise not solid.
Yet it is further driven by the wolf of delusion, as ignorance sears and boils day and night.
Knowing only how to crave water and grass, the mind and spirit are entangled by external objects.

How can one fail to repent, yet claim that merely giving away wealth will suffice? To outwardly conceal crooked speech while hoping to escape prior transgressions—would hell then have no business with such people?
Expecting to be reborn in heaven, there are indeed those of this sort in the world.
The path of darkness is not like this: Unless one ceases to create karma, One must uproot the source of transgression.
When the root is empty and defilements are unreal, Internally and externally, causes and conditions are severed.
Accumulated sins, as vast as mountains and peaks, Are ignited all at once by the fire of wisdom; In an instant they turn to ash, And for eternal kalpas, no smoke remains.
When deluded, the three realms exist; upon awakening, one escapes the clamorous entanglements. When the mind leaves no trace within the six sense bases, it is pure and reaches the source.
Hell becomes a land of purity; I beckon you to part from the various heavens and bid farewell to the abodes of the three miserable paths.
There is no further affinity with you; it matters not whether it be early or late.
Awakening to principle is the boundless mind;
suchness itself is sitting. The suchness of objects is dhyāna; suchness remains utterly unmoving.
The Great Way has neither center nor periphery; if one can penetrate it in this way, this is what is called the lotus in fire.
Non-seeking is the Dharma-eye; The presence of thought, conversely, becomes a demon. Non-seeking and further non-thought—this is Amitābha.
True Suchness is shared with the Bodhisattvas; In total, there is nothing more to compare.
When the three mountains of iron are smelted away, And the five peaks of copper are melted down, The forest withers and the birds naturally disperse.
The ocean dries up and fish and dragons perish; Without a teacher, one breaks the precepts. When the Dharma exists, all is empty; Bodhisattvas have no afflictions.
Sentient beings frown out of attachment; Without the conditions for affliction, there is no thief.
To be deceived by a thief, one need not ask a master; The King of the Mind should know this for itself.
The wise person contemplates wealth and beauty, Realizing they are illusory and empty. Using food and clothing merely to sustain life, he exhorts others to study the Suchness (Tathatā).

When the time came, he moved his hermitage away; Having nothing left to fill his stores, He saw that ordinary people are greedily attached to worldly affairs And cannot escape the cycle of the three realms. Thus, for their sake, he taught the principle of non-arising.
Closing their ears, they pretend not to hear; such skulls as these—on what day will they emerge from the clamor of dust?
Wall-paintings waste their colors in vain; it would be better than a Buddha of empty voids. Abiding in the Dharma, one is like the non-abiding within the aggregates, facing the bright sun.
Do not believe in words of existence or non-existence; look instead to the *pāramitās*.
When seeing, it is as if not seeing; when hearing, it is as if not hearing; when rejoicing, it is as if not rejoicing; when angry, it is as if not angry.
All things return entirely to Suchness (*tathatā*). Spontaneously, there is neither self nor person.
One’s fast must be the fast of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*); one’s precepts must be the precepts of the true mark. To maintain the fast and precepts with signs (*nimitta*) is not so.
In the end, all returns to decay; decay belongs to impermanence. How can one escape the three realms?

If the mind-king does not understand its own affairs, then even if you go to a famous mountain, it will be of no avail. Even if you were to behold a Buddha image, in truth it would have nothing to do with you.
It is like a monkey seeing the moon in the water; only upon trying to grasp the moon does one realize the difficulty.
Seeking liberation through conditioned phenomena, one has no prospect of escape for kalpas on end. One must directly enter the rational nature to achieve Buddhahood;
of this there is no doubt. Although one may not receive a formal prediction, seeing that one is a child of the World-Honored One, the Buddha dispatches one to extinguish birth and death.
Yet birth and death continue to follow long after; if one does not study the marks of a Great Being, [one remains bound].
Yet acting like a young grandson, you hold fast to the mind while seeking further for a Buddha. Is this not foolishness?
To be reviled by others for no reason—pretend not to hear; let your tongue not move and your mind not be provoked to anger.
When there are no obstructions at the passes and barriers, you are one who has emerged from the entanglements.
True Suchness is originally without marks; That which is attained belongs to the stream of ordinary beings.
In the past we were father and son; having grown up, we went abroad. Today we have met again and seen one another:
The father is young while the son has white hair. One lifetime’s bonds have been untied; The whole body sleeps within the sack, And in the heart there is no conscious awareness.
The ears are not pulled by ropes; the mind is fundamentally without bondage. Even when mingling with the dust of the world, there is no clamor.
If you wish to attain true liberation, take up the sword and slay the ox. When the ox is dead, the man perishes as well.
There is no need to seek even the Buddha; sit with your whole body within emptiness, and you will immediately cross over the stream of birth and death.
Gazing to the horizon at the realm before me, it is desolate and without a single person; Turning my head to look behind, even my shadow does not follow my body.
If you do not begrudge letting go of greed and hatred, It is all in vain to read the commentaries on the Śāstras; It is like studying medical prescriptions while refusing to take the medicine.
From where does illness arise?
To grasp at emptiness is to grasp at form; to grasp at form is for form to be impermanent. Form is empty and not mine;
sitting upright, I see my hometown.

The essence of the sutra is fundamentally nameless; in its reception and upholding, there is neither form nor sound. The mind relies upon the principle of signlessness—this is truly the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When the grandson was crying, the mother said, "Come, I will give you gold," yet he merely grasped another's yellow leaf.
Immediately, with a composed voice,
he shed tears that formed rivers and seas; his bones became like Mount Vipula, solely because of the dharmas of sensory consciousness,
for which reason he sent forth his mind.
If another person has some business, I still feign ignorance; how much more so when others ask nothing of me?

You who possess slanderous tongues and are stubbornly base—exhort your teacher with a lion’s roar! Do not learn the howling of a jackal; if you can rise like a fragrant elephant, [you shall be known].
Moved by fortune, a phoenix came to welcome him;
In one kind of scholarly pursuit, he likewise entered the examination hall. Yet because his oral explanations were faltering, he was ranked among the failures and remained in a foreign land.
The mind-king does not understand its own affairs, And is instead driven by the six thieves. Working with the thieves, there is no way to escape birth and death.
One who distinguishes others will never be base; One who discerns jewels will never be poor— Such is the man of iron who carries his burden right now.

Reluctant to trade for gold or silver, the ten directions gather in a single assembly; each person studies non-action (*wuwei*). This is the place where Xuanfu dwells with a mind empty, returning as a successful candidate.
There are sons who refuse to marry, and daughters who refuse to wed; father and son sit together in harmony, discussing the discourse on non-arising.
The four elements share one house; the three bodies share one chamber. All evil associates—

In general, see that the Buddha Amitābha teaches you this one Dharma: where there is a matter, there is no place to avoid it; if you can practice according to principle and preserve the fundamental nature, then there will be benefit.
The Way is the path of non-action; Yet those who cultivate it rely on action. If one relies on the provisional, there is no counting;
In the midst of the real, true reality is rare.
Seeking nothing is superior to prostrating before the Buddha; Contentment is superior to observing the fast. Fundamentally, there has never been firewood for the fire.

Why trouble yourself further gathering firewood when the truth fills the world? Entering into principle is truly not so difficult; yet you are constantly bound by conditioned phenomena—on what day will you see Amitābha?
When arising, only dharmas arise; when acting, one acts together with the Buddha. Within the three realms, all dharmas are naturally unborn—a great ocean vast and boundless.
Sentient beings bind themselves in shackles, yet they do not seek to escape this wondrous virtue.
When the mind gives rise to weary calculations regarding the sands [of the Ganges],
a single thought-moment of pure clarity causes lotus flowers to bloom everywhere; for every flower is a pure land,
and every pure land is a Tathāgata.
Seven-character verse:
Three hundred and sixty states of the Great Tang. I have briefly set myself free to wander according to my inspiration;
In a mere instant, I know all affairs to their end. If one speaks of entering into principle, it is even more profound and subtle.
Partaking of clear water with external acquaintances, It is all but empty, boneless delusion.
Yet one returns to the paths of the eastern and western mountains; Without abandoning causes and conditions, one rides upon an ox.
Looking back, the green mountains are as level as the palm of a hand; Looking forward, the Han River flows toward the east.
I ask you, Nāṭaputra of the Western Regions: In your diligent pursuit of the Bequeathed Dharma, you sought nothing for yourself;
Yet you entered the great ocean to return to the burning house, Unaware that you were traveling through the air and had lost your ox.
If anyone sees me returning to the Eastern Land, Tell them that I originally resided at the head of the Western Sea.
Coming and going spontaneously without obstruction, Entering and exiting birth and death—what cause for sorrow?
Without thought and without recollection, this is true emptiness; Within the wondrous virtue of the Dharma-body, one sees for oneself.
Responding to capacities and engaging with beings, one accords with true wisdom; Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it flows everywhere.
Thoroughly penetrating the non-existence of self and persons, and the non-existence of phenomena;
Since persons and phenomena leave no trace of activity, the conscious spirit is naturally free from obstruction.
Pervading the entire realm of sands like empty space, there is no need for sitting meditation or upholding precepts; Transcending in liberation, how could it require effort or merit?
The names and marks of bodhi and prajñā are provisional; Nirvāṇa and suchness are likewise empty.
If you wish for the mind and spirit to attain true liberation, All names and marks are originally non-existent.
The winds and dust of the worlds in the ten directions are purified; In every prefecture and county, all hardships and perils have ceased.
The Way of Kings is vast and open, free from partiality or factionalism; All sentient beings throughout the land are of one suchness, unmoving.
Without raising weapons, he brings peace to the myriad people; The Dharma King joins his palms like a jewel atop his topknot.
In the void, he spontaneously beholds the cool moon, Whose single light shines universally through the Sahā world.
This light is serene, without coming or going; Neither increasing nor decreasing, it is without birth or cessation.
Thus, Wondrous Virtue manifests his true body; In a single instant, he does not arise for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Boundless and inexhaustible like space, Space is boundless and ineffable.
But if one is personally without mind regarding the myriad things, what hindrance can there be to the myriad things constantly surrounding one?
The Iron Ox does not fear the lion’s roar; he is just like a wooden man who beholds flowers and birds.
The essential nature of the wooden man is inherently without sentiment; when flowers and birds encounter him, they too are not startled.
The state of mind is suchness; it is simply this. Why worry that the path to Bodhi will not be accomplished?
It is pure, unconditioned, and free from the dust of consciousness. Without discarding the physical body, one is the wondrous Dharma-body.
Only because sentient beings possess tainted habitual tendencies, you temporarily dwell in a grass hut to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Wheel of Dharma turns constantly, yet no one sees it; The Udumbara flower appears but once in an age.
The wondrous Dharmakāya of formless true emptiness Has remained unchanged through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Seek not the Buddha, nor seek the person; Simply within your own mind, do not harbor greed or anger.
The diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion are suddenly exhausted; this is the very essence of the Tathāgata.
Within, there is no defilement; without, there is no dust. In the midst, it is vast and open, without gates or fords;
the spirit dwells without obstruction within the three realms, just like a crystal sphere situated within the solar disk.
If the mind-king understands by relying on true wisdom, all existence and non-existence are simultaneously cast aside.
The body follows the worldly flow, yet the mind does not flow; night comes and the eyes sleep, but the mind does not sleep.
Heaven and hell are both devoid of sentience; one reaches this profound and mysterious ground through spontaneous ease.
I tell you, people of the world, do not be so foolish and deluded; Dwell for a time in this thatched hut as a mere expedient.
Once you have no thoughts of food, clothing, or warmth, There is no need to crave the things of this world.
This body is an illusory transformation, like the flame of a lamp; In an instant it will be gone without notice—then the head will be to the south.
All who seek with effort labor in vain; To conceptualize the Truth is truly to cling to form and emptiness.
A deviation of a hair’s breadth loses one a thousand li; Throughout kalpa after kalpa of birth, the Way is difficult to penetrate.
With a deluded mind, they hope to escape beyond the Three Realms, Yet they do not know they are already within the Iron Ring Mountains.
The twelve divisions of the sūtras, together with the precepts and rules—clinging to these forms, one constantly upholds them according to the texts;
thus, life after life, one obtains only conditioned fruits. Following along within the three realms, there is no time of escape.
If one can leave behind such signs and enter directly into the principle, within that principle there is neither thought nor reflection.
Within the *pātra* leaves lies the *udumbara* flower; all myriad phenomena are as one family.
In joyful picking the flower, one does not see the fruit; in auspiciously gathering the fruit, one does not observe the flower.
The conditions of its original source were never known; the Dharma King scorns them as being like rice or hemp.
An old country man enters a village; His eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all lost.
Searching within and without, he finds no trace; His former dwelling is empty and silent.
Returning to the hall, he asks the Empty King: "Is it all here that one learns non-action?"
Yellow leaves drift and fall, turning to dust; Originally neither false nor true.
The dwelling-place of sentient beings holds the hues of autumn; The nameless gentleman is serene in spring.
Do not speak of the pearls within the Dragon Palace— From the beginning, my words have been different from yours.
An empty fist is merely what an infant believes; how could it be used to deceive an old man?
When deluded, the heart’s craving for desire is like fire; when the mind opens and realizes the principle, the fire turns to ash.
Ash and fire are originally of one essence; know that when delusion is exhausted, one is the Tathāgata.
Truly, this family is so poor it possesses not a single thing; these words all emerge from within the void.
When speaking, one must return to the source; I dare not disobey the Buddhas of the past.
Father and son sit together in the empty mountains, formless and as they are, dwelling amidst the temporal.
The world sees stillness, yet fundamentally there is no stillness; Though appearing idle, even at leisure one is not idle.
The eighty-four thousand [dharmas] share a single principle; Differences in phenomena are merely established as distinct names.
The twelve Vedas and their commentaries— Be diligent in the three and six, and do not give rise to them.
The lands of the ten directions are all my dwelling; The elder’s great gate is always open.
Those with discernment stand guard outside the courtyard; Only those without a [discriminating] mind enter the principle and see the Tathāgata.
The people of the world love the false and do not love the true; The people of the world pity the wealthy yet loathe the poor.
Venerating only the three miserable realms and the eight impurities, While turning one's back on the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body— There is no other path to transcend birth and death.
The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are all of one kind:
When extended, they pervade the lands of the ten directions; When withdrawn, they reside within a single hair-tip.
There is but a single gate without a key; Its expansion and contraction, its rising and falling, are said to be right and wrong.
Only those who can proclaim the principle of non-arising Possess these skillful means, for they also follow this path.
Those of the two vehicles all say they are not capable, But those of superior caliber possess profound wisdom.
If you wish to attain the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, O Householder, there is nothing superior to being free from attachment to things and having no mixed thoughts.

The path of practice is easy; the path of practice is easy. Whether internal, external, or intermediate, rely upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Since fundamental wisdom is devoid of sentient characteristics, phenomena do not arise.
Non-arising is precisely the entry into the True Principle. Neither form nor mind, it emits a single ray of light; the *udumbara* flower in the void manifests within the ground of the mind.
This is called wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is the Honored One. When the mind and wisdom penetrate in unison, one reaches the original source.

All things return together to the Gate of Non-duality. Existence is not existence, yet the Principle eternally abides; non-existence is not non-existence, for there is no root of existence. Thus it is with all Buddhas of the future as well.

Thus it is. The present is identical to the ancient World-Honored Ones; throughout the three periods of time, there has never been a divergent path. Buddha after Buddha has transmitted it to one another until it has been passed down to this day.
Without "other" externally and without "self" internally, one accords with Buddha-wisdom without raising a blade of grass. To penetrate the Buddha-way is to act without action.

The Way does not abandon the conditioned activities of ordinary beings; yet the names and marks of the conditioned are all empty flowers. Without name and without mark, one transcends birth and death.
I have a great robe that is not of worldly silk; though dyed with myriad colors, it is unstained, crystalline and pure like unbleached linen.

When cutting it, no knife was used; when sewing it, no thread was used. Constantly worn and never parted from the body, though some may not see it themselves, it shields against cold and heat throughout the three thousandfold world-system, covering all that is insentient and sentient.
If one can obtain and maintain this great robe, having put it on, one enters directly into the Hall of the Empty King. Si-si, di-si-si—sighing at one’s own pair of eyebrows, one speaks to him.
Sitting in a sublime place, one knows nothing at all of the myriad affairs. If the six consciousnesses resemble the eyebrows, one immediately attains the inconceivable.
If the six consciousnesses resent the eyebrows, then in discussing the matter, one is submerged in brain-folly. If you were to remove the eyebrows, you would be deceived by the people of the world;

Leaving one room and entering another, coming and going, you were made to weep. This coming and going was solely due to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Now that you have attained awakening, you must know contentment; with contentment, you shall always reach the original source.

Without cause, you lose your mind and run to the gate to search for it. You inquire of old acquaintances, but all is silent; there is no trace to be found.
Returning to the hall, you examine and contemplate deeply; you change your perception of sentient beings and call it peace of mind.
Unable to go outside to seek out teachers, you enter nirvana within your own home. Great man! That which existed in the past is gone today; your household affairs have collapsed.
Having exhausted [all debts], he ransomed a group of slaves. There were six servants and masters; each had six dependents, making thirty-six in total.

Peaceful. Clearly and distinctly seeing the suffering of the three realms, worldly fame is irrelevant.

Do not seek further; the present does not abide. Do not let thoughts intrude from moment to moment; the future has not yet arrived, so do not anticipate it in advance.

Since there are no three periods of time, the mind is identical to the Buddha-mind. To act in silent accordance with emptiness is itself the profound practice; therein is not even the slightest dharma.

Whatever meets the eye is accepted with equanimity; there are no precepts to maintain and no defilements to purify. One penetrates deeply into the empty mind, for phenomena possess neither life nor duration.
If one can act thus, one will attain ultimate, perfect penetration.

Mazu replied, “Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River with a single draught, and then I will tell you.”
"You say: 'The great ocean waves of Old Master Gui of Donglin are shallow;
the square inch of the petty man’s mind is deep. When the sea dries up, its bottom will finally be seen.'"
